subject: mathematics
question_text: Determine whether f(x) = log(x + √(x² + 1)) is even or odd.

mark_split.label: The domain, and the product that gives 1
Show f(−x) = −f(x) and name the parity

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.15, chapter 2 FUNCTIONS, Very Short Answer question 26(ii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 shape gives one mark to the product (−x + √(x² + 1))(x + √(x² + 1)) = 1, which is the idea the whole question turns on, and one to the logarithm law that finishes it. The domain condition is part of the answer: x + √(x² + 1) is positive for every real x because √(x² + 1) > |x|, so the domain is R and the parity test is meaningful; that is written in the lines, not only here. The result does not depend on the base of the logarithm, since log(1/u) = −log u in any base, and the card says so. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1–Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would decide this — why the logarithm is defined everywhere, and the product you multiply to simplify f(−x).

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Domain, then the product
steps.margin_note: One mark for the domain line and the product. The product is the whole idea; write it out in full before using it.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply x + √(x² + 1) by its conjugate −x + √(x² + 1). The squares cancel and only 1 is left.
lines: so x + √(x² + 1) > 0 and the domain is R.

recall.must_convey: That √(x² + 1) is greater than |x| so x + √(x² + 1) > 0 and the domain is R, and that the conjugate product (−x + √(x² + 1))(x + √(x² + 1)) equals 1.
accept: root of x squared plus one is bigger than the size of x so the bracket is always positive
the log is defined for every real x so the domain is R
multiply by the conjugate minus x plus root x squared plus one
the product is x squared plus one minus x squared which is one
conjugate tho multiply cheste root square minus x square equals one vasthundi
reject: log of one over u is minus log u
f of minus x is minus f of x

steps.why: Two things have to be settled before any parity claim. First the logarithm needs a positive argument, and √(x² + 1) > |x| makes x + √(x² + 1) positive for every real x, so the domain is R and −x is always in it. Second, the conjugate product is 1, which is what lets f(−x) be written as a reciprocal.
common_mistakes: Skipping the domain line and assuming a logarithm is always defined.
Writing √(x² + 1) as x + 1, which is not the same.
Expanding the product as x² + 1 + x² instead of x² + 1 − x².

steps.label: Use the logarithm law
steps.margin_note: The second mark is log(1/u) = −log u and the word. Write f(−x) = −f(x) explicitly, then name the function odd.
steps.memory_tip: A reciprocal inside a logarithm comes out as a minus sign: log(1/u) = −log u, in any base.
lines: This holds in any base, since log(1/u) = −log u
is true for every base of the logarithm.

lines.text: ∴ f is an odd function on R.

recall.must_convey: That log of a reciprocal is minus the logarithm, so f(−x) = −log(x + √(x² + 1)) = −f(x), which makes f an odd function.
accept: log of one over u is minus log u
so f of minus x is minus log of x plus root x squared plus one
that is exactly minus f of x
log reciprocal ante minus log kabatti f of minus x equals minus f of x, odd function
reject: so f of minus x equals f of x

steps.why: The reciprocal from the previous step is exactly what the logarithm law needs: log(1/u) = −log u, so the whole value flips sign and nothing else changes. A numerical check agrees — f(0.6) = 0.5688 and f(−0.6) = −0.5688, and f(1.7) = 1.3008 and f(−1.7) = −1.3008.
common_mistakes: Writing log(1/u) as 1/log u instead of −log u.
Stopping at −log(x + √(x² + 1)) and not saying that this is −f(x).
Naming the function even because the expression contains x².
